reflection: Across the five frozen models, the initial libraries show small average cost reductions but high variance and frequent failures in high-demand trajectories (e.g., seed 11 trajectory 3, seed 12 trajectory 3, seed 14 trajectory 3). The main failure mode is that pipeline-aware relaxation rules trigger too often when pipeline is high relative to recent demand, but recent demand is a delayed block mean that can lag a sudden surge. This causes under-ordering during demand emergencies, increasing downstream backlog and total cost. Conversely, backlog-service rules can over-order when backlog is high but pipeline is already sufficient, creating upstream inventory and backlog. The rules also lack coordination between nodes: a reduction at node 0 can starve node 1 and node 2 after the pipeline delay, while extra orders at node 1 can create upstream backlog at node 2. The best-performing candidate (initial2) uses more conservative guards (recent > 0) and slightly different thresholds, but still fails in high-demand scenarios. The worst cases show cost increases up to 2.7 per period. The predicted selection examples indicate that the library is often not chosen over zero, suggesting that the corrections are not reliably beneficial. To improve, rules should be more conservative in reducing orders when backlog exists anywhere, and should avoid increasing orders when pipeline is already high relative to recent demand. Also, the growth feature is noisy due to block mean repetition; using it to trigger increases can be harmful. Future candidates should focus on small, coordinated corrections that protect downstream service, especially when backlog is present, and should avoid large deltas based on pipeline ratios alone.
memory: Key lessons: (1) Pipeline-aware relaxation must be conditional on low backlog; if backlog > 0, do not reduce orders. (2) Backlog-service increases should be capped and only when pipeline is truly thin (pipeline < recent). (3) Growth-based rules are unreliable due to delayed block mean; avoid using growth to trigger increases. (4) Corrections should be small (<=2) and symmetric across nodes to avoid starving downstream. (5) Zero correction is often chosen; rules must be clearly beneficial in high-demand states. (6) Use guards for zero demand (recent > 0). (7) Avoid increasing orders when pipeline > 2*recent even if backlog exists, as it may create upstream backlog. (8) Focus on protecting downstream service: when backlog > 0 and pipeline < recent, add 1-2; when pipeline > 3*recent and backlog == 0, subtract 1-2. (9) Do not use growth > threshold to add orders; instead use backlog and pipeline directly.

The dominant failure mode is under-ordering during demand emergencies: pipeline-aware relaxation triggers when pipeline is high relative to recent delivered demand, but recent is a delayed block mean that lags a sudden surge, so the rule trims exactly when service protection is needed, raising downstream backlog and total cost. The second failure mode is over-ordering when backlog is high but pipeline is already adequate, which creates upstream inventory and backlog at node 2. memory: Key lessons: (1) Never reduce orders when backlog > 0; pipeline relaxation only when backlog == 0. (2) Backlog-service increases only when pipeline is truly thin (pipeline < recent) and capped at 1-2. (3) Avoid growth-based triggers; growth from repeated block means is noisy and can cause overreaction. (4) Keep deltas small (<=2) and symmetric across nodes to avoid starving downstream after pipeline delay. (5) Guard all rules with recent > 0 to avoid division by zero and zero-demand artifacts. (6) Do not increase orders when pipeline > 2*recent even if backlog exists, as it creates upstream backlog. (7) Zero correction is often selected; rules must be clearly beneficial in high-demand states to be chosen. (8) Focus on protecting downstream service: when backlog > 0 and pipeline < recent, add 1-2; when pipeline > 3*recent and backlog == 0, subtract 1-2. (9) Use backlog and pipeline directly rather than growth ratios. (10) Coordinate nodes: upstream reductions can starve downstream after 4 periods, so only reduce when local backlog is zero and pipeline is clearly excessive.
